Three months later, a further several hundred roles were slashed, mostly at Pixar and National Geographic, followed by a couple hundred in tech and HR in September. No sooner had the latest layoffs been announced than their potential impact on Disney's portfolio of 12 theme parks came into the spotlight. That's because the parks are the crown jewels of the Experiences division along with Disney's cruise ships, its in-park merchandise operation and a few remaining high street stores. The global licensing and publishing arm of Disney Consumer Products escaped the cuts as it was moved from Experiences to the studio division at the start of this month. Disney's ambitious development pipeline The layoffs were revealed in an article by the Los Angeles Times, which said they had been confirmed by a person familiar with the matter who was not authorised to comment publicly. Deadline added that it had been told the cuts are "mostly project-based, as the division constantly must reprioritize and schedule based on the workflows of multiple projects across its mandate." This sounded ominous given how many projects are in the Experiences division's pipeline. Disney lifted the curtain on its current development drive in 2023 when it announced that it was nearly doubling its capital expenditure on Experiences to approximately $60bn over the next decade. It soon announced major new attractions at all of its resorts along with the construction of multiple new cruise ships. Indeed, Disney gave the green light to so many new developments that in March last year its then-chief executive Bob Iger said: "We have more projects underway around the world than at any time in our history." Disney didn't stop there as just two months later it announced plans to develop a new theme park in Abu Dhabi. Although local leisure operator Miral is due to build and operate the complex, it will be designed by Disney's Imagineers, who are named after their imaginative use of engineering. Miral is covering the cost of the Imagineers working on the project, but they are employed by Disney and, in Iger's own words, they already had more work on their hands than ever before. Theme parks are labour-intensive businesses and, as testimony to this, the Experiences division has a total of 185,000 employees. Cutting the workforce by 200 would be a reduction of just 0.1%, so, at first glance, it seems hard to understand how this could affect the future of the parks. However, of course, it depends on who is being let go. The Imagineers have more impact than others on upcoming attractions, and 159 of them are being laid off, according to a notice filed by Disney in the wake of the two articles. Disney's Experiences division drives profits Disney did not comment in the articles, but soon after they were published, Imagineers started posting on LinkedIn confirming the news. "After eleven years at Walt Disney Imagineering, the last two on staff as Story Lead, I have been bitten by the layoff bug as of the end of the year," wrote Michael Crawford. "After an incredible chapter with Walt Disney Imagineering, my time with the company has come to an unexpected close as part of a layoff," added graphic designer Xavier Treto. It fuelled online speculation about the future of projects in Disney's pipeline, compounded by the recent revelation that attendance at Disney's North American parks remained flat last year, according to data from the Themed Entertainment Association (TEA). However, that didn't stop the Experiences division from giving a magic touch to Disney's bottom line. Experiences are the engine behind Disney's blockbuster profits, and in the year to 27 September 2025 they generated just over a third of the company's $94.4 billion revenue and a staggering 57% of its $17.6 billion operating income. In August, Disney forecast a "high single-digit" percentage increase in the Experiences division's 2026 operating income, which raises the question of why it needs to make further cost cuts. Getting a sense of how much money the layoffs will save requires knowing the Imagineers' total wage bill and the number of them on Disney's books. However, the costs and headcount of Disney's design division are part of its overall expenses and aren't itemised separately in its filings with the New York Stock Exchange. This has kept the Imagineers' average salary a closely-guarded secret. Until now. Disneyland Paris provides a rare insight Disneyland Paris is an exception to this rule, and there is good reason for this. It dates back to the opening of Disneyland in California in 1955, which soon became such a success that motels and restaurants began springing up next to the park, breaking the immersive atmosphere. To prevent a repeat of this in France, Disney requested a vast plot of land which would enable it to maintain standards throughout the entire resort, from the parks to the surrounding hotels and even the roads and nature reserves. It came with a catch. Disneyland Paris comprises seven on-site hotels, two convention centres, a 27-hole golf course and two theme parks - the recently-renamed Disney Adventure World and the neighbouring Disneyland Park, which was the first to swing open its ornate iron gates in 1992. The entire complex is around a fifth the size of Paris, but Disney hasn't got free rein over all of the land. The sprawling site was originally home to five villages and huge beet fields which were earmarked for development until the 1973 oil crisis put them on ice. Mindful of the fact that it was selling so much land near to its capital to a foreign corporation, the French government only agreed to hand it over to Disney on condition that it entered into a public-private partnership. In order to ensure that the land was developed in accordance with the government's vision, Disney committed to partnering with the public urban management authority, EPAFrance. The French government only sells the land to Disney in stages once previous plots have been developed and approved by EPAFrance, which enables the government to guarantee that they will benefit the local area. In order to retain its rights to the land, Disney has to develop it by specific deadlines, which also ensures that the resort is regularly upgraded. EPAFrance represents the public while Disney is the private party in the partnership. Reflecting this structure, when the resort opened, its parent company Euro Disney was listed on the Euronext stock exchange with only 49% of the shares in Disney's hands and the remainder owned by the public. This gave it considerable disclosure obligations, and the same applies to the suite of other entities that Disney set up to support it. These obligations include filing publicly available accounts which lift the lid on precisely how much has been spent on staff and how many people are employed. Inside the operations of Disneyland Paris Until 2023, two companies were involved with the design of Disneyland Paris. S.E.T.E.M.O. Imagineering provided studies and supervised the construction of the theme park attractions, while Euro Disneyland Imagineering (EDLI) was responsible for the management and administration of the overall design of the parks as well as their construction. The structure was simplified in 2023 when EDLI was deregistered, and S.E.T.E.M.O. changed its name to EDLI to become the master design company of Disneyland Paris. The division is run by David Wilson, who initially joined Disney in 1991 after serving six years in the US Navy as a nuclear engineering officer. There are 393 people in his team according to EDLI's accounts for the year ending 30 September 2025, when development was in full swing on the biggest-ever expansion to the resort. It is a stark illustration of the hole it could leave if 200 Imagineers were laid off, but that's not all. The accounts reveal that the staff costs came to a total of £36.9m (€42.3m), putting the annual average per person at £93,893. This would give a total saving of £14.9m ($20m) from the 159 layoffs, and although this may seem a lot to you or me, it only represents around 0.09% of the Experiences division's $23.3 billion annual costs, which seems too small to be material. Calculating the cost of Disney's job cuts Of course, this calculation is based on the pay of Imagineers in Paris, whereas Disney's notice says the layoffs will be at its Glendale, California campus. However, the team in Paris essentially works for the same division of Disney as their counterparts in California, so you would expect there to be a degree of wage parity. Cost of living and cultural standards are of course different in France and the United States, though it is important to note that the employees at Disneyland Paris are amongst the most well-remunerated of any Disney resort, thanks partly to the tough labour laws in the country. In fact, as blooloop has reported, the staff in Paris are the only Disney employees worldwide who share in the profits of the theme parks they work for. So, if anything, you might expect the average pay to be lower in California than in Paris, and the lower it is, the less material the savings from the layoffs would be. Even if the opposite were true and the average cost of every employee in California is actually double that of Paris, it would only come to 0.18% of the Experiences division's costs, which is still minuscule. In summary, although the layoffs concern a relatively large number of people, it appears they generate an extremely small saving. Accordingly, it seems hard to understand the benefit of the cuts, especially at a time when Disney presumably needs all hands on deck because it has more projects in the pipeline than ever before. Under these circumstances, redeployment would surely seem to make more sense than redundancy. Of course, the cuts would make perfect sense if they relate to a project which Disney has not firmly committed to and is no longer in a position to proceed with, but none of the announced attractions seems to fit the bill. The alternative is that the Imagineers who have been laid off may have been working on unannounced projects which are no longer going ahead, and if so, we may never get confirmation of what they were. Time will tell.

headline: Discriminated Unions in TypeScript
snippet: Earlier, we looked at how custom type guards (value is Type) let you manually inspect unknown data and teach TypeScript its shape. But what if you have a set of known object types that share a common property? Enter Discriminated Unions (sometimes called tagged unions or algebraic data types). They are one of the most powerful patterns in TypeScript because TypeScript does the type narrowing for you automatically—no custom guard function required. 1. What is a Discriminated Union? A discriminated union is a combination of three things: Types with a common property (the discriminant or "tag"), where each type has a unique literal type for that property. A union of those types. A conditional check (like a switch statement) on that discriminant property. Let’s see it in action with a classic real-world scenario: asynchronous state management. 2. Practical Example: State Management Imagine you are building a component that fetches data from an API. At any given moment, your state can be in one of three phases: Loading, Success, or Error. If you lump everything into one giant interface with optional fields (data?: User, error?: string), you open the door to impossible states (like having both data and an error, or neither). Instead, model them as a discriminated union using a status tag: interface IdleState { status: "idle"; } interface LoadingState { status: "loading"; interface SuccessState { status: "success"; data: { id: number; name: string }; // Only exists on success! interface ErrorState { status: "error"; error: Error; // Only exists on error! type FetchState = IdleState | LoadingState | SuccessState | ErrorState; 3. Automatic Narrowing in Action When you consume a discriminated union, you can use a simple switch or if statement checking the status tag. Watch how TypeScript's control flow analysis automatically figures out what properties are safe to access: function renderUI(state: FetchState) { switch (state.status) { case "idle": return " Press button to fetch. "; case "loading": Loading data... case "success": return ` Welcome, ${state.data.name} `; case "error": Error: ${state.error.message} No as SuccessState type assertions, no manual in checks, and no runtime ambiguity. The literal type of status tells TypeScript precisely which branch of reality your code is operating in. 4. Pro-Tip: Exhaustiveness Checking with never What happens if you add a new state later (like RetryingState), but forget to update your switch statement? In JavaScript, your UI might silently fail or render nothing. You can force TypeScript to catch missing cases at compile time using the never type: Summary Custom Type Guards are your best tool when dealing with untrusted, unstructured data coming from the outside world (unknown inputs). Discriminated Unions are your best tool when designing internal application logic, state machines, and data structures where you control the shapes.

headline: Two details worth checking in a paginated ASP.NET Core CRUD
snippet: This article was prepared with AI assistance and is based on a local ASP.NET Core and SQL Server demo. The examples are excerpts, not a complete application or a production-readiness claim. A customer CRUD can look complete when creating, editing, and deleting work from the UI. Two less visible details deserve a closer look: what happens when sort values are equal, and what happens when two requests try to create the same email address. 1. Give pagination a fully specified order The demo keeps query execution in an EF Core repository. The application service bounds the page size before passing the query to it: { Page = Math. Clamp(query. Page, 1, int. MaxValue / size), PageSize = size }; The upper page bound keeps the subsequent integer offset calculation from overflowing. Clamping is a contract choice: an API could reject invalid inputs instead, provided that behavior is documented for its callers. In the repository, each supported ordering includes the unique ID as a second key. For example: data = data. OrderBy(x => x. Name).ThenBy(x => x. Id); .Skip((query. Page - 1) * query. PageSize) .Take(query. PageSize) .ToListAsync(ct); Sorting only by name leaves the relative order of customers with the same name unspecified. Adding the ID gives those ties an explicit order. This does not make offset pagination a consistent snapshot. Inserts and deletes between page requests can still shift records. Count and item queries are separate database operations too, so concurrent writes can make their results disagree. The example does not solve either issue; those requirements would need a separate design decision. 2. A duplicate check does not enforce uniqueness The application checks whether an email already exists before saving. That gives the common duplicate case a useful response, but two requests can both pass the check before either commits. The database therefore also has a unique index on Email. Infrastructure translates SQL Server's uniqueness errors into an exception defined by Application: await db. SaveChangesAsync(ct); } catch (DbUpdateException ex) when (ex. InnerException is SqlException { Number: 2601 or 2627 }) throw new DuplicateEmailException(ex); Application handles that exception, and the API returns HTTP 409 for the duplicate email case. Application does not need to reference SqlException or EF Core. There is an important limit in this small implementation: the translation assumes a uniqueness failure during this save means a duplicate email. If another unique constraint is added, that assumption must be revisited to avoid reporting the wrong error. What was checked, and what remains open The recorded local SQL Server test submitted ten concurrent creates with the same email. It returned one 201 and nine 409 responses. The HTTP smoke test also covered CRUD, filters, sorting, and pagination. These are results from a previous local verification, not an independent installation or a complete correctness proof. The project separates domain entities, application services and interfaces, infrastructure implementations, and API composition. That separation makes the SQL-specific translation easy to locate. It does not remove the need to test the behavior against SQL Server. For a small business application, when would you move from offset pagination to keyset pagination? And how do you identify the exact violated constraint when a repository has several unique keys?

headline: New DWP bank checks aim to save £1.2bn by tackling benefit fraud and errors
snippet: The new system covers Universal Credit, Pension Credit and Employment and Support Allowance. The DWP estimates that fraud and error involving undeclared savings and time spent abroad cost £1.5bn in 2025-26. The eligibility verification measure is expected to generate £1.2bn in savings by 2030-31. The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has issued its first Eligibility Verification Notice, requiring banks and other financial institutions to check information relating to certain benefit-receiving accounts as part of a new effort to tackle fraud and incorrect payments. The system applies to Universal Credit, Pension Credit and Employment and Support Allowance (ESA). It is designed to identify cases where claimants may have savings that affect their entitlement or have spent longer abroad than benefit rules permit. However, the new powers do not give DWP officials direct access to people's bank accounts, transaction histories or spending habits. Instead, financial institutions will be asked to check relevant accounts against specified eligibility criteria and flag cases that may require further investigation. A flag does not mean that someone has committed fraud or broken benefit rules. The Government has also stressed that no decision about a person's benefit entitlement can be made solely on the information supplied through the system. Undeclared savings and overseas stays under scrutiny Undeclared savings and the time claimants spend outside the UK are among the areas targeted by the new checks. The DWP estimates that fraud and error involving undeclared savings and time spent abroad in relation to Universal Credit and Pension Credit cost taxpayers £1.5bn in 2025-26. The Eligibility Verification Measure is expected to deliver £1.2bn in savings by 2030-31. Minister for Innovation, Fraud and Debt Lilian Greenwood said: “Benefit fraudsters should be looking over their shoulder. These new powers will help us crack down on those who deliberately abuse the system, while ensuring people receive the right support at the right time. “We are not interested in where people do their weekly shop or how much they’re spending on new clothes. Banks will simply be asked to identify if somebody may no longer meet the rules for the benefits they receive, allowing us to investigate further where necessary. “With £1.2 billion in savings expected by 2030/31, this is a major step forward in tackling fraud and error, protecting public money and ensuring support goes to those who genuinely need it.” Anyone flagged through the system will not automatically have their benefits stopped. The DWP says further enquiries will be necessary before any action is taken. The measure is initially being introduced through a test-and-learn phase and will be subject to independent oversight before any wider rollout. Wider crackdown on benefit fraud The powers were introduced under the Public Authorities (Fraud, Error and Recovery) Act 2025 and form part of the Government's wider efforts to reduce incorrect benefit payments and protect public funds. The Government is also planning to deploy an additional 2,000 anti-fraud specialists to Jobcentres and introduce tougher checks involving Universal Credit claims from people who have travelled abroad. The wider package of measures is expected to save taxpayers £14.6bn over the next five years. For claimants, the distinction between an eligibility flag and a finding of wrongdoing will be important as the new system develops. The DWP says the checks are intended to identify cases for further investigation, rather than automatically penalise people receiving benefits.
